units.excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is our first version of a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from powerful capabilities of future foundation models.
units.paraphrase: This is the first version of a protocol set intended to address severe risks from powerful future foundation model capabilities.

units.excerpt: In focusing on these risks at the model level, it is intended to complement Google's existing suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enable AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is meant to complement existing safety practices and support innovation consistent with Google's AI Principles.

units.excerpt: In the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which models may pose severe risks (which we call "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)"), and articulate a spectrum of mitigation options to address such risks.
units.paraphrase: The Framework defines protocols to detect capability levels posing severe risk, called Critical Capability Levels, and lays out mitigation options.

units.excerpt: We are starting with an initial set of CCLs in the domains of Autonomy, Biosecurity, Cybersecurity, and Machine Learning R&D.
units.paraphrase: The initial CCLs cover Autonomy, Biosecurity, Cybersecurity, and Machine Learning R&D domains.

units.excerpt: Risk assessment in these domains will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, and scientific understanding.
units.paraphrase: Assessing risk in these domains requires evaluating cross-cutting capabilities like agency, tool use, and scientific understanding.

units.excerpt: We will be expanding our set of CCLs over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
units.paraphrase: The set of CCLs will grow as experience and insight into future model capabilities increase.

units.excerpt: We aim to have this initial framework implemented by early 2025, which we anticipate should be well before these risks materialize.
units.paraphrase: The lab aims to implement this initial framework by early 2025, ahead of anticipated risk materialization.

units.excerpt: The Framework is exploratory and based on preliminary research, which we hope will contribute to and benefit from the broader scientific conversation.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is described as exploratory, based on preliminary research intended to engage with the wider scientific community.

units.excerpt: It will be reviewed periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
units.paraphrase: The Framework will be periodically reviewed and is expected to change substantially as understanding improves.

units.excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Responsible Capability Scaling. The core components of Responsible Capability Scaling are to:
units.paraphrase: The Framework draws on the broader discourse on Responsible Capability Scaling, whose core components follow.

units.context_stem: The core components of Responsible Capability Scaling are to:
units.excerpt: Identify capability levels at which AI models pose heightened risk without additional mitigations
units.paraphrase: One component is identifying capability levels that pose heightened risk absent mitigation.

units.context_stem: The core components of Responsible Capability Scaling are to:
units.excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels
units.paraphrase: Another component is implementing detection protocols for those capability levels.

units.context_stem: The core components of Responsible Capability Scaling are to:
units.excerpt: Prepare and articulate mitigation plans in advance for when such capability levels are attained
units.paraphrase: A third component is preparing mitigation plans in advance of reaching those capability levels.

units.context_stem: The core components of Responsible Capability Scaling are to:
units.excerpt: Where appropriate, involve external parties in the process to help inform and guide our approach.
units.paraphrase: Where appropriate, external parties should be involved to inform and guide the approach.

units.excerpt: We are piloting this initial version of the Frontier Safety Framework as a first step to operationalizing these principles.
units.paraphrase: This initial version is a pilot, the first step toward operationalizing the stated principles.

units.excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/blog/2023-09-26-rsp/, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/preparedness/
units.paraphrase: Footnote listing external references on frontier AI safety and responsible scaling.

units.excerpt: This section describes the central components of the Frontier Safety Framework.
units.paraphrase: This section introduces the Framework's central components.

units.excerpt: The Framework is built around capability thresholds called "Critical Capability Levels." These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, models may pose heightened risk.
units.paraphrase: The Framework centers on capability thresholds, called CCLs, at which models may pose heightened risk without mitigation.

units.excerpt: We determine CCLs by analyzing several high-risk domains: we identify the main paths through which a model could cause harm, and then define the CCLs as the minimal set of capabilities a model must possess to do so.
units.paraphrase: CCLs are determined by identifying harm pathways in high-risk domains and defining the minimal capabilities needed to cause that harm.

units.excerpt: We have conducted preliminary analyses of the Autonomy, Biosecurity, Cybersecurity and Machine Learning R&D domains. Our initial research indicates that powerful capabilities of future models seem most likely to pose risks in these domains.
units.paraphrase: Preliminary analysis of four domains suggests future model capabilities are most likely to pose risk there.

units.excerpt: The CCLs we have identified are described below.
units.paraphrase: The identified CCLs are described later in the document.

units.excerpt: The capabilities of frontier models are tested periodically to check whether they are approaching a CCL.
units.paraphrase: Frontier model capabilities are periodically tested to check proximity to a CCL.

units.excerpt: To do so, we will define a set of evaluations called "early warning evaluations," with a specific "pass" condition that flags when a CCL may be reached before the evaluations are run again.
units.paraphrase: Early warning evaluations will be defined with a pass condition flagging potential CCL attainment before the next evaluation round.

units.excerpt: We are aiming to evaluate our models every 6x in effective compute and for every 3 months of fine-tuning progress.
units.paraphrase: The goal is to evaluate models at every 6x increase in effective compute and every 3 months of fine-tuning progress.

units.excerpt: To account for the gap between rounds of evaluation, we will design early warning evaluations to give us an adequate safety buffer before a model reaches a CCL.
units.paraphrase: Early warning evaluations will be designed to provide a safety buffer accounting for gaps between evaluation rounds.

units.excerpt: When a model reaches evaluation thresholds (i.e. passes a set of early warning evaluations), we will formulate a response plan based on the analysis of the CCL and evaluation results.
units.paraphrase: Upon reaching evaluation thresholds, a response plan will be formulated using CCL analysis and evaluation results.

units.excerpt: We will also take into account considerations such as additional risks flagged by the review and the deployment context.
units.paraphrase: Additional considerations like flagged risks and deployment context will also inform the response.

units.excerpt: The initial version of the Framework focuses on two categories of mitigations: security mitigations to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and misuse filtering, detection, and response) to manage access to and prevent the expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
units.paraphrase: This version focuses on security mitigations against weight exfiltration and deployment mitigations to control access to critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: We have developed frameworks for Security Levels and Deployment Levels to enable calibrating the robustness of mitigations to different CCLs.
units.paraphrase: Security Levels and Deployment Levels frameworks were developed to calibrate mitigation robustness to different CCLs.

units.excerpt: A model may reach evaluation thresholds before mitigations at appropriate levels are ready.
units.paraphrase: It is possible for a model to reach evaluation thresholds before adequate mitigations are ready.

units.excerpt: If this happens, we would put on hold further deployment or development, or implement additional protocols (such as the implementation of more precise early warning evaluations for a given CCL) to ensure models will not reach CCLs without appropriate security mitigations, and that models with CCLs will not be deployed without appropriate deployment mitigations.
units.paraphrase: If mitigations are not ready in time, deployment or development would be paused, or additional protocols implemented, to ensure models do not reach or deploy at CCLs without proper mitigations.

units.excerpt: Figure 1 depicts the relationship between these components of the Framework.
units.paraphrase: Figure 1 shows the relationship among the Framework's components.

units.excerpt: "Autonomy" captures the potential misuse of AI models with significant capacity for agency and flexible action/tool use over long time horizons and across multiple domains.
units.paraphrase: Footnote defining Autonomy as covering misuse of models with agency and flexible tool use across long horizons and domains.

units.excerpt: Effective compute is a measure of the performance of a foundation model that uses scaling laws to integrate model size, dataset size, algorithmic progress, and compute into a single metric.
units.paraphrase: Footnote defining effective compute as a scaling-law-based composite metric of model performance factors.

units.excerpt: While there is no direct relationship between effective compute and model size, a rough estimate suggests that a 6x increase in effective compute would correspond to approximately 2-2.5x increase in model size.
units.paraphrase: Footnote noting a rough correspondence: 6x effective compute increase approximates 2-2.5x model size increase.

units.excerpt: More specifically, the early warning evaluations will be a set of model evaluations that we are confident will be passed before the model is 6x in effective compute or 3 months of fine-tuning away from the CCL.
units.paraphrase: Footnote specifying that early warning evaluations are expected to be passed well before a model is within 6x effective compute or 3 months of fine-tuning from the CCL.

units.excerpt: Figure 1: the relationship between different components of the Framework.
units.paraphrase: Caption for Figure 1 describing the relationship between Framework components.

units.excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework proposes two kinds of mitigations to address models with critical capabilities: security mitigations to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations to manage access to/prevent the expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
units.paraphrase: Two mitigation types are proposed: security mitigations against weight exfiltration and deployment mitigations to manage access to critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: For each category of mitigation, we have developed several levels of mitigations, allowing us to calibrate the robustness of measures to the risks posed.
units.paraphrase: Several mitigation levels have been developed per category to calibrate robustness to the risk posed.

units.excerpt: The table below describes levels of security mitigations that may be applied to model weights to prevent their exfiltration.
units.paraphrase: The following table lists security mitigation levels applicable to model weights to prevent exfiltration.

units.excerpt: This is an important measure because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by bad actors) to any critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Preventing weight exfiltration matters because released weights could allow safeguard removal and access to critical capabilities by bad actors.

units.locator: Security Table / Level 0 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 0: Status quo; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 0: Status quo
units.paraphrase: Security Level 0 is labeled Status quo.

units.excerpt: Industry standard development and enterprise controls. E.g., multi-factor authentication, basic access control mechanisms, secure software development standards, red-team tests.
units.paraphrase: Level 0 measures include standard industry development and enterprise controls such as MFA, access controls, secure development standards, and red-team tests.

units.locator: Security Table / Level 1 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 1: Controlled access; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 1: Controlled access. Access Control List hygiene. Non-forgeable lineage of models. Approximately RAND L3.
units.paraphrase: Security Level 1, Controlled access, involves ACL hygiene and non-forgeable model lineage, approximately RAND L3.

units.excerpt: Limited access to raw representations of the most valuable models, including isolation of development models from production models. Specific measures include model and checkpoint storage lockdown, SLSA Build L3 for model provenance, and hardening of ML platforms and tools.
units.paraphrase: Level 1 measures limit access to valuable model representations, isolate development from production, and include storage lockdown, SLSA Build L3 provenance, and ML platform hardening.

units.locator: Security Table / Level 2 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 2: Lockdown of unilateral access; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 2: Lockdown of unilateral access. Significant restrictions of unilateral access of model weights. Approximately RAND L3-L4.
units.paraphrase: Security Level 2 significantly restricts unilateral access to model weights, approximately RAND L3-L4.

units.context_stem: Row: 2: Lockdown of unilateral access; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Changes to ML platforms and tools to disallow unilateral access to raw model representations outside the core research team, with exceptions granted on the basis of business need.
units.paraphrase: Level 2 measures disallow unilateral access to raw model representations outside the core team, except by business-need exception.

units.locator: Security Table / Level 3 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 3: High-trust developer environments; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 3: High-trust developer environments. For developers with unilateral access to raw models, protection against exfiltration and account compromise. Approximately RAND L4.
units.paraphrase: Security Level 3 provides protection against exfiltration and account compromise for developers with unilateral raw model access, approximately RAND L4.

units.context_stem: Row: 3: High-trust developer environments; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Models can be accessed only through high-trust developer environments (HTDE), hardened, tamper-resistant workstations with enhanced logging.
units.paraphrase: Level 3 restricts model access to hardened, tamper-resistant HTDE workstations with enhanced logging.

units.excerpt: See https://www.rand.org/pubs/working_papers/WRA2849-1.html.
units.paraphrase: Footnote reference to a RAND working paper.

units.locator: Security Table / Level 4 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 4: Advanced protection; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 4: Advanced protection. Model weights are generally not accessible to humans, even non-unilaterally. Hardened software platforms and confidential-compute hardware make it difficult even for well-funded adversaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities. Approximately RAND L5.
units.paraphrase: Security Level 4 makes model weights generally inaccessible to humans, using hardened platforms and confidential-compute hardware, approximately RAND L5.

units.excerpt: Minimal trusted computing base (TCB). TPUs with confidential compute capabilities. Dedicated hardware pods for training and serving high-value models.
units.paraphrase: Level 4 measures include a minimal trusted computing base, confidential-compute TPUs, and dedicated hardware pods for high-value models.

units.excerpt: This table below describes levels of deployment mitigations that may be applied to models and their descendants to manage access to and limit the expression of critical capabilities in deployment.
units.paraphrase: The following table describes deployment mitigation levels applicable to models and derivatives to manage access to critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: Critical capabilities may have closely associated positive capabilities, misuse of critical capabilities may be more or less difficult to distinguish from beneficial uses, and the overall risks of misuse may differ by deployment context.
units.paraphrase: Critical capabilities may closely relate to beneficial uses, and misuse risk can vary by deployment context, complicating distinction.

units.excerpt: Because of this, the mitigation options listed below are illustrative and will need to be tailored to different use cases and risks.
units.paraphrase: The listed mitigation options are illustrative and require tailoring to specific use cases and risks.

units.locator: Deployment Table / Level 0 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 0: Status quo; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 0: Status quo
units.paraphrase: Deployment Level 0 is labeled Status quo.

units.excerpt: Safety finetuning of models and filters against general misuse and harmful model behavior.
units.paraphrase: Level 0 deployment measures consist of safety fine-tuning and filters against general misuse and harmful behavior.

units.locator: Deployment Table / Level 1 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 1: Mitigations targeting the critical capability; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 1: Mitigations targeting the critical capability. Use of the full suite of mitigations to prevent the inappropriate access of critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Deployment Level 1 uses a full mitigation suite to prevent inappropriate access to critical capabilities.

units.context_stem: Row: 1: Mitigations targeting the critical capability; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Application, where appropriate, of the full suite of prevailing industry safeguards targeting the specific capability, including safety fine-tuning, misuse filtering and detection, and response protocols.
units.paraphrase: Level 1 measures apply industry-standard safeguards targeting the specific capability, including fine-tuning, filtering, detection, and response.

units.context_stem: Row: 1: Mitigations targeting the critical capability; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Periodic red-teaming to assess the adequacy of mitigations.
units.paraphrase: Periodic red-teaming assesses whether mitigations remain adequate.

units.locator: Deployment Table / Level 2 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 2: Safety case with red team validation; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 2: Safety case with red team validation. Targeted safeguards, aimed at keeping numbers of incidents below a prespecified amount, with pre-deployment validation by a red-team.
units.paraphrase: Deployment Level 2 uses targeted safeguards to keep incidents below a prespecified amount, validated by red-teaming before deployment.

units.context_stem: Row: 2: Safety case with red team validation; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: A robustness target is set based on a safety case considering factors like the critical capability and deployment context.
units.paraphrase: A robustness target is derived from a safety case that considers the capability and deployment context.

units.context_stem: Row: 2: Safety case with red team validation; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Afterwards, similar mitigations as Level 1 are applied, but deployment takes place only after the robustness of safeguards has been demonstrated to meet the target.
units.paraphrase: Level 1-like mitigations are applied, but deployment occurs only after safeguards are shown to meet the robustness target.

units.context_stem: Row: 2: Safety case with red team validation; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Some protection against inappropriate internal access of the critical capability, such as automated monitoring and logging of large-scale internal deployments, Security Level 2.
units.paraphrase: Some internal-access protection is provided, such as automated monitoring/logging of large-scale internal deployments, at Security Level 2.

units.locator: Deployment Table / Level 3 / Level and capabilities
units.context_stem: Row: 3: Prevention of access; Column: Level and capabilities
units.excerpt: 3: Prevention of access. Mitigations that allow for high levels of confidence that capabilities cannot be accessed at all.
units.paraphrase: Deployment Level 3 provides high confidence that capabilities cannot be accessed at all.

units.context_stem: Row: 3: Prevention of access; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Technical options for this level of deployment safety are currently an open research problem.
units.paraphrase: Technical means to achieve this level of deployment safety are still an open research problem.

units.context_stem: Row: 3: Prevention of access; Column: Measures
units.excerpt: Highly restricted and monitored internal use, alongside high security.
units.paraphrase: Level 3 involves highly restricted, monitored internal use combined with high security.

units.excerpt: Critical Capability Levels describe thresholds at which models may pose heightened risk without additional mitigation.
units.paraphrase: CCLs are thresholds where models may pose heightened risk absent additional mitigation.

units.excerpt: We will develop early warning evaluations to detect when models approach CCLs, and apply appropriate mitigations to models that reach evaluation thresholds.
units.paraphrase: Early warning evaluations will be developed to detect CCL approach, and appropriate mitigations applied at evaluation thresholds.

units.excerpt: Note: when we refer to a model's capabilities, we include capabilities resulting from any reasonably foreseeable fine-tuning and scaffolding to turn the model into a functioning system.
units.paraphrase: Footnote clarifying that model capabilities include those from reasonably foreseeable fine-tuning and scaffolding.

units.excerpt: The table below details an initial set of CCLs we have identified through a preliminary analysis of the Autonomy, Biosecurity, Cybersecurity, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.
units.paraphrase: The table below presents an initial set of CCLs identified via preliminary analysis of four risk domains.

units.excerpt: As we conduct further research into these and other risk domains, we expect these CCLs to evolve and for several CCLs at higher levels or in other risk domains to be added.
units.paraphrase: As research continues, these CCLs are expected to evolve and new CCLs at higher levels or other domains to be added.

units.excerpt: Autonomy: Risks of the misuse of AI models with significant capacity for agency and flexible action/tool use over long time horizons and across many domains.
units.paraphrase: The Autonomy domain covers risks from misuse of models with significant agentic capacity and flexible tool use over long horizons and many domains.

units.locator: CCL Table / Autonomy / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Autonomy; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Autonomy level 1: Capable of expanding its effective capacity in the world by autonomously acquiring resources and using them to run and sustain additional copies of itself on hardware it rents.
units.paraphrase: Autonomy level 1 is defined as capability of autonomously acquiring resources to run and sustain additional self-copies on rented hardware.

units.excerpt: A model at this capability level could, if misused, pose difficult-to-predict and large-magnitude risks.
units.paraphrase: If misused, a model at Autonomy level 1 could pose unpredictable, large-magnitude risks.

units.excerpt: Its adaptability would enable harmful activity via many means, and its ability to act autonomously and expand its effective capacity means its activity could be scaled significantly without being hindered by resource constraints.
units.paraphrase: Its adaptability enables harm through many means, and autonomous capacity expansion allows scaling without resource constraints.

units.excerpt: If misused or supported by well-equipped bad actors, such activity may be especially difficult to constrain.
units.paraphrase: If misused or supported by well-equipped bad actors, the activity may be especially hard to constrain.

units.excerpt: Biosecurity: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation and/or execution of a biological attack.
units.paraphrase: The Biosecurity domain covers risks of models assisting the development, preparation, or execution of a biological attack.

units.locator: CCL Table / Bio amateur enablement / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Bio amateur enablement level 1; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Bio amateur enablement level 1: Capable of significantly enabling a non-expert to develop known biothreats that could increase their ability to cause severe harm compared to other means.
units.paraphrase: Bio amateur enablement level 1 is defined as significantly enabling a non-expert to develop known biothreats increasing severe harm capability.

units.locator: CCL Table / Bio amateur enablement / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Bio amateur enablement level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: Many biothreats capable of causing significant amounts of harm are currently out of the reach of non-experts because of lack of knowledge about their potential for harm and the methods of their acquisition and misuse.
units.paraphrase: Many harmful biothreats are currently inaccessible to non-experts due to knowledge gaps about harm potential and acquisition/misuse methods.

units.locator: CCL Table / Bio amateur enablement / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Bio amateur enablement level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: An LLM that helps overcome these knowledge gaps, e.g. by suggesting plausible attack strategies or providing detailed instructions for the development of a bio agent, could significantly increase society's vulnerability to fatal attacks by malicious amateurs.
units.paraphrase: An LLM that closes these knowledge gaps by suggesting attack strategies or instructions could greatly increase societal vulnerability to fatal amateur attacks.

units.locator: CCL Table / Bio expert enablement / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Bio expert enablement level 1; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Bio expert enablement level 1: Capable of significantly enabling an expert (i.e. PhD or above) to develop novel biothreats that could result in an incident of high severity.
units.paraphrase: Bio expert enablement level 1 is defined as significantly enabling a PhD-level expert to develop novel biothreats causing a high-severity incident.

units.locator: CCL Table / Bio expert enablement / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Bio expert enablement level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: A very small number of bio agents have the potential to cause harm of an exceptional magnitude.
units.paraphrase: A very small number of bio agents could cause exceptionally severe harm.

units.locator: CCL Table / Bio expert enablement / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Bio expert enablement level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: The discovery of enhancements to these agents, or of agents of comparable harmfulness, could increase the chances of a very severe bio attack or accident.
units.paraphrase: Discovering enhancements to these agents, or comparably harmful agents, could raise the likelihood of a severe bio attack or accident.

units.excerpt: Cybersecurity: Risks of models assisting in the execution of a cyber attack.
units.paraphrase: The Cybersecurity domain covers risks of models assisting in executing cyberattacks.

units.locator: CCL Table / Cyber autonomy / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Cyber autonomy level 1; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Cyber autonomy level 1: Capable of fully automating opportunistic cyberattacks on organizations with a limited security posture.
units.paraphrase: Cyber autonomy level 1 is defined as capable of fully automating opportunistic cyberattacks against weakly secured organizations.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber autonomy level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: Harmful cyberattacks against organizations with limited security posture can already be carried out by individuals with limited expertise, but the automation of such attacks would significantly lower the costs of doing so, and moreover would enable the execution of such attacks at scale.
units.paraphrase: Such attacks are already possible by low-expertise individuals, but automation would lower costs and enable execution at scale.

units.locator: CCL Table / Cyber enablement / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Cyber enablement level 1; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Cyber enablement level 1: Capable of enabling an amateur to carry out sophisticated and severe attacks (e.g. those that disrupt critical national infrastructure).
units.paraphrase: Cyber enablement level 1 is defined as enabling an amateur to carry out sophisticated, severe attacks such as disrupting critical infrastructure.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber enablement level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: Severe cyberattacks against high-impact targets currently require significant expertise and effort across the cyber kill-chain to carry out.
units.paraphrase: Severe attacks on high-impact targets currently need significant expertise and effort across the cyber kill chain.

units.context_stem: Row: Cyber enablement level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: Increasing text generation, programming, and tool-use capabilities in models, combined with improved understanding of cyber offense strategies, could help amateurs overcome difficult steps in the planning and execution of attacks.
units.paraphrase: Growing model capabilities in text generation, programming, tool use, and cyber offense understanding could help amateurs overcome difficult attack steps.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D / Risk domain
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D; Column: Risk domain
units.excerpt: Machine Learning R&D: Risks of the misuse of models capable of accelerating the rate of AI progress, the result of which could be the unsafe attainment or proliferation of other powerful AI models.
units.paraphrase: The ML R&D domain covers risks of models accelerating AI progress, potentially leading to unsafe attainment or proliferation of powerful AI.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D level 1 / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D level 1; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Machine Learning R&D level 1: Could significantly accelerate AI research at a cutting-edge lab if deployed widely, e.g. improving the pace of algorithmic progress by 3X, or comparably accelerate other AI research groups.
units.paraphrase: ML R&D level 1 is defined as significantly accelerating cutting-edge AI research if widely deployed, e.g. a 3x boost to algorithmic progress.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D level 1 / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: The mismanagement of a model with these capabilities could enable the proliferation of cutting-edge AI systems to malicious actors by enabling their AI development in turn.
units.paraphrase: Mismanaging a model with these capabilities could enable proliferation of cutting-edge AI to malicious actors via their own AI development.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D level 1 / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D level 1; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: This could result in increased possibilities of harm from AI misuse, if AI models at that point were exhibiting capabilities like the ones described in other CCLs.
units.paraphrase: This could increase harm possibilities from AI misuse if models exhibit capabilities described in other CCLs at that time.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D level 2 / Critical capability level
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D level 2; Column: Critical capability level
units.excerpt: Machine Learning R&D level 2: Could fully automate the AI R&D pipeline at a fraction of human labor costs, potentially enabling hyperbolic growth in AI capabilities.
units.paraphrase: ML R&D level 2 is defined as fully automating the AI R&D pipeline at a fraction of human labor cost, potentially enabling hyperbolic AI capability growth.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D level 2 / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D level 2; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: This could give any actor with adequate computational resources the ability to reach capabilities more powerful than those in the other CCLs listed in a short amount of time.
units.paraphrase: This could let any actor with sufficient compute reach more powerful capabilities than other listed CCLs quickly.

units.locator: CCL Table / ML R&D level 2 / Rationale
units.context_stem: Row: Machine Learning R&D level 2; Column: Rationale
units.excerpt: The mismanagement of a model with these capabilities could result in the proliferation of increasingly and unprecedentedly powerful systems, resulting in significant possibilities of harm via misuse.
units.paraphrase: Mismanaging such a model could cause proliferation of unprecedentedly powerful systems, creating significant misuse harm potential.

units.excerpt: We aim to have this initial framework implemented by early 2025, which we anticipate should be well before these risks materialize.
units.paraphrase: The lab aims for full implementation by early 2025, ahead of anticipated risk materialization.

units.excerpt: The Framework is exploratory and based on preliminary research.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is described as exploratory and grounded in preliminary research.

units.excerpt: We expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves, and we will publish substantive revisions as appropriate.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is expected to change substantially with improved understanding, with substantive revisions to be published as needed.

units.excerpt: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
units.paraphrase: The following issues are intended to be addressed in future Framework versions.

units.context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
units.excerpt: Greater precision in risk modeling: Given the nascency of the underlying science, there is significant room for improvement in understanding the risks posed by models in different domains, and refining our set of CCLs.
units.paraphrase: One future issue is improving precision in risk modeling given the immaturity of the underlying science, refining understanding of domain risks and CCLs.

units.context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include: Greater precision in risk modeling
units.excerpt: We also intend to take steps to forecast the arrival of CCLs to inform our preparations.
units.paraphrase: There is also an intention to forecast CCL arrival to inform preparations.

units.context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
units.excerpt: Capability elicitation: We are working to equip our evaluators with state of the art elicitation techniques, to ensure we are not underestimating the capability of our models.

excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from powerful capabilities of foundation models.
paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols addressing severe risks from powerful foundation model capabilities.

excerpt: It is intended to complement Google’s existing suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enable AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's existing AI safety practices and supports innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.
paraphrase: The Framework draws on the wider discourse regarding Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.

excerpt: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
paraphrase: This introduces the list of core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Identify capability levels at which AI models without additional mitigations could pose severe risk
paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels at which unmitigated models could pose severe risk.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels
paraphrase: Another core component is implementing protocols to detect when such capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Prepare and articulate mitigation plans in advance of when such capability levels are attained
paraphrase: Another core component is preparing mitigation plans before such capability levels are reached.

context_stem: The core components of Frontier AI Safety Frameworks are to:
excerpt: Where appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide our approach.
paraphrase: Another core component is involving external parties, where appropriate, to inform and guide the approach.

excerpt: In version 2.0 of the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which models may pose severe risks (which we call “Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)”), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
paraphrase: Version 2.0 specifies detection protocols for Critical Capability Levels and mitigation approaches for them.

excerpt: At present, the Framework primarily addresses misuse risk, but we also include an exploratory section addressing deceptive alignment risk, focusing on capability levels at which such risks may begin to arise.
paraphrase: The Framework mainly covers misuse risk but also has an exploratory section on deceptive alignment risk.

excerpt: For each type of risk, we define here a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them.
paraphrase: For each risk type, the document defines CCLs and a corresponding mitigation approach.

excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities like agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

excerpt: The safety of frontier AI systems is a global public good.
paraphrase: Frontier AI safety is characterized as a global public good.

excerpt: The protocols here represent our current understanding and recommended approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
paraphrase: The protocols reflect the current understanding and recommended approach for anticipating and addressing severe frontier AI risks.

excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to AI systems reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly applied across AI systems reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: These mitigations should be understood as recommendations for the industry collectively: our adoption of them would only result in effective risk mitigation for society if all relevant organizations provide similar levels of protection, and our adoption of the protocols described in this Framework may depend on whether such organizations across the field adopt similar protocols.
paraphrase: The mitigations are framed as industry-wide recommendations, and Google's own adoption may depend on similar adoption by other organizations.

excerpt: The Framework is exploratory and based on early research.
paraphrase: The Framework is described as exploratory and grounded in early research.

excerpt: We may change our approach and recommendations over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
paraphrase: Google may revise its approach and recommendations as it gains more insight into future frontier model capabilities.

excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
paraphrase: Google commits to periodic review of the Framework and expects it to evolve substantially.

excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/blog/2023-09-26-rsp/, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/preparedness/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/updates/issue-brief-components-of-frontier-ai-safety-frameworks/,
paraphrase: A footnote listing external references on frontier AI safety practices.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
paraphrase: Misuse risk is defined as threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of highly autonomous systems purposefully undermining human control over AI systems.
paraphrase: Deceptive alignment risk is defined as highly autonomous systems purposefully undermining human control.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: delineating when such capability becomes present, and subsequently when the initial mitigation for this capability—automated monitoring—is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: This describes delineating when a capability arises and when automated monitoring, its initial mitigation, ceases to be adequate.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We intend to evaluate our most powerful frontier models regularly to check whether their AI capabilities are approaching a CCL.
paraphrase: Google intends to regularly evaluate its most powerful frontier models to check proximity to a CCL.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We also intend to evaluate any of these models that could indicate an exceptional increase in capabilities over previous models, and where appropriate, assess the likelihood of such capabilities and risks before and during training.
paraphrase: Google also intends to evaluate models showing exceptional capability increases and, where appropriate, assess risks before and during training.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: To do so, we will define a set of evaluations called “early warning evaluations,” with a specific “alert threshold” that flags when a CCL may be reached before the evaluations are run again.
paraphrase: Google will define early warning evaluations with alert thresholds flagging approaching CCLs before the next evaluation cycle.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to equip the model with appropriate scaffolding and other augmentations to make it more likely that we are also assessing the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model.
paraphrase: Evaluations aim to equip models with scaffolding and augmentations so downstream system capabilities are also captured.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust the alert threshold of our evaluations if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
paraphrase: Google may increase evaluation frequency or adjust alert thresholds if progress suggests the safety buffer is insufficient.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: Where necessary, early warning evaluations may be supplemented by other evaluations to better understand model capabilities relative to our CCLs.
paraphrase: Additional evaluations may supplement early warning evaluations when needed to clarify capabilities relative to CCLs.

section_heading: 2 - Assessing the Capabilities of Frontier Models
excerpt: We may use additional external evaluators to test a model for relevant capabilities, if evaluators with relevant expertise are needed to provide an additional signal about a model’s proximity to CCLs.
paraphrase: External evaluators may be used to test models when specialized expertise is needed to gauge proximity to CCLs.

excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
paraphrase: Upon reaching an alert threshold, Google will assess proximity to the CCL and analyze risk, involving experts as needed.

excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
paraphrase: The assessment informs the formulation and application of a response plan.

excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in this document.
paraphrase: Most response plans will center on applying the mitigations described later in the document.

excerpt: For misuse, we have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and misuse filtering, detection, and response) intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: Misuse mitigations fall into two categories: security mitigations preventing weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations countering misuse in deployment.

excerpt: For deceptive alignment risk, automated monitoring may be applied to detect and respond to deceptive behavior for models that meet the first deceptive alignment CCL.
paraphrase: For deceptive alignment risk, automated monitoring may be used for models meeting the first deceptive alignment CCL.

excerpt: Note that these mitigations reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
paraphrase: The mitigations address only severe capability risks; other considerations may lead to stricter mitigations than the Framework specifies.

excerpt: A model flagged by an alert threshold may be assessed to pose risks for which readily available mitigations (including but not limited to those described below) may not be sufficient.
paraphrase: A flagged model may pose risks that available mitigations cannot sufficiently address.

excerpt: If this happens, the response plan may involve putting deployment or further development on hold until adequate mitigations can be applied.
paraphrase: In such cases, the response plan may pause deployment or development until adequate mitigations exist.

excerpt: Conversely, where model capabilities remain quite distant from a CCL, a response plan may involve the adoption of additional capability assessment processes to flag when heightened mitigations may be required.
paraphrase: If a model remains far from a CCL, the response plan may add capability assessment processes to flag when stronger mitigations are needed.

excerpt: The appropriateness and efficacy of applied mitigations should be reviewed periodically, drawing on information like related misuse or misuse attempt incidents; results from continued post-mitigation testing; statistics about our intelligence, monitoring and escalation processes; and updated threat modeling and risk landscape analysis.
paraphrase: Mitigation appropriateness and efficacy should be periodically reviewed using incident data, post-mitigation testing, monitoring statistics, and updated threat modeling.

excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse CCLs, as well as the mitigations that we provisionally assess as appropriate for them.
paraphrase: This introductory statement outlines that the Misuse section covers mitigation approach, misuse CCLs, and provisional appropriate mitigations.

excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in deployments.
paraphrase: Misuse mitigations fall into security mitigations against exfiltration and deployment mitigations against misuse in deployment.

excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
paraphrase: Multiple levels of security mitigations allow calibrating robustness to the level of risk.

excerpt: For deployment mitigations, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
paraphrase: Deployment mitigations follow a standard process to apply, assess, and review measures calibrated to CCLs, reflecting their iterative nature.

excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration risk are important for models reaching CCLs.
paraphrase: Security mitigations against exfiltration are important for models that reach CCLs.

excerpt: This is because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Weight release could allow removal of safeguards and give threat actors access to critical capabilities.

excerpt: Here, we rely on the RAND framework to articulate the level of security recommended for each CCL.
paraphrase: The RAND framework is used to articulate recommended security levels for each CCL.

excerpt: When we reference RAND security levels, we are referring to the security principles in their framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
paraphrase: References to RAND security levels denote the framework's security principles, not its concrete benchmark measures.

excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
paraphrase: As AI security is actively evolving research, the concrete measures for each security level are expected to change substantially.

excerpt: The following deployment mitigation process will be applied to models reaching a CCL, allowing for iterative and flexible tailoring of mitigations to each risk and use case.
paraphrase: A deployment mitigation process will be applied to models reaching a CCL, allowing flexible tailoring by risk and use case.

excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
paraphrase: Step one is developing and assessing mitigations, with safeguards and a safety case built through iteration.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability. This includes, as appropriate, safety fine-tuning, misuse filtering and detection, and response protocols.
paraphrase: Sub-step: developing and improving safeguards targeting the capability, including fine-tuning, filtering, detection, and response protocols as appropriate.

context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through assurance evaluations and threat modeling research. The assessment takes the form of a safety case, taking into account factors such as the likelihood and consequences of misuse.
paraphrase: Sub-step: assessing mitigation robustness via assurance evaluations and threat modeling, producing a safety case considering likelihood and consequences of misuse.

excerpt: Pre-deployment review of safety case: general availability deployment of a model takes place only after the appropriate corporate governance body determines the safety case regarding each CCL the model has reached to be adequate.
paraphrase: Step two: general availability deployment occurs only after a corporate governance body deems the safety case for each reached CCL adequate.

excerpt: Post-deployment review of safety case: the safety case will be updated through red-teaming and revisions to our threat models.
paraphrase: Step three: the safety case is updated post-deployment via red-teaming and revised threat models.

excerpt: The safeguards for the model may be updated as well to ensure continued adequacy.
paraphrase: Model safeguards may also be updated to maintain continued adequacy.

excerpt: The table below details a set of CCLs we have identified through ongoing analysis of the CBRN, Cyber, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.
paraphrase: The table describes CCLs identified from analysis of CBRN, Cyber, and Machine Learning R&D risk domains.

excerpt: We expect these to evolve over time.
paraphrase: The CCLs are expected to evolve over time.

excerpt: We recommend a security level to each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.
paraphrase: Each CCL is assigned a recommended security level reflecting the minimum appropriate security the frontier AI field should apply.

excerpt: In practice, our overall security posture may commonly exceed the baseline levels recommended here.
paraphrase: Actual security posture may often exceed the recommended baseline levels.

excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking and may be adjusted if our empirical understanding of the risks changes.
paraphrase: Recommended security levels reflect current thinking and may be adjusted as empirical understanding evolves.

excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other widely available models that have not demonstrably caused or contributed to severe risks, or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
paraphrase: Adjustment might occur if a model's capabilities aren't meaningfully different from other benign widely-available models, or if open release benefits are judged to outweigh risks.

excerpt: Relatedly, we believe these recommendations will only be effective if the entire frontier AI field applies them, and of limited social utility if not.
paraphrase: The recommendations are believed effective only if adopted across the entire frontier AI field.

excerpt: Therefore, we recommend models at this level of capability have exceptional security even though they may have substantial innovation costs.
paraphrase: Exceptional security is recommended for such models despite substantial innovation costs.

excerpt: Note that we have removed the Autonomy risk domain, which was included in Frontier Safety Framework version 1.0.
paraphrase: The Autonomy risk domain from version 1.0 has been removed.

excerpt: Most of the advanced risk that was captured by this CCL is now covered by our misalignment section.
paraphrase: Most advanced risk formerly captured by this CCL is now covered under the misalignment section.

excerpt: From the perspective of misuse risks, our threat models suggest that no heightened deployment mitigations would be necessary, and that security controls and detection at a level generally aligned with RAND SL 2 would be adequate.
paraphrase: For misuse risks, threat models suggest no heightened deployment mitigations are needed and RAND SL 2 security is adequate.

excerpt: For example, through the use of a self-replicating CBRN agent. Compared to a counterfactual of not using generative AI systems.
paraphrase: Example given: a self-replicating CBRN agent, compared against a counterfactual of no generative AI use.

excerpt: E.g. deletion or exfiltration of critical information, or destroying or disabling key systems.
paraphrase: Examples of end-to-end cyberattacks include deleting/exfiltrating critical information or disabling key systems.

excerpt: E.g. deletion or exfiltration of sensitive information/disruption of key systems of organizations with strong security posture, or the creation of predictable and large-scale effects on critical national infrastructure.
paraphrase: Examples of high impact cyber attacks include disruption of strongly secured organizations or large-scale effects on critical infrastructure.

excerpt: Relative to the counterfactual of using 2024 AI technology and tooling.
paraphrase: The order-of-magnitude comparison is relative to 2024 AI technology and tooling.

excerpt: This section describes an initial approach for addressing risks of deceptive alignment.
paraphrase: This section presents an initial approach to addressing deceptive alignment risks.

excerpt: By "deceptive alignment," we mean the risk that AI systems purposefully undermine human control over AI systems.
paraphrase: Deceptive alignment is defined as AI systems purposefully undermining human control.

excerpt: While we do not express any opinion here about how likely it is for deceptive alignment to arise, this section’s provisions aim to prepare for this possibility.
paraphrase: No view is expressed on the likelihood of deceptive alignment, but the section aims to prepare for the possibility.

excerpt: Note that the effective mitigation of deceptive alignment risk requires the application of safeguards to all AI systems reaching critical capabilities.
paraphrase: Effective mitigation of deceptive alignment risk requires safeguards across all AI systems reaching critical capabilities.

excerpt: It is important that the industry adopts strategies for addressing this risk: what is detailed in this section represents one possible approach for doing so.
paraphrase: Industry-wide adoption of strategies is important; this section presents one possible approach.

section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
excerpt: An initial mitigation approach focuses on detecting when models might develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which they have the potential to undermine human control, assuming no additional mitigations were applied.
paraphrase: The initial approach focuses on detecting a baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could enable undermining human control absent mitigations.

section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
excerpt: When models reach this capability level, we believe applying an automated monitor to the model’s explicit reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought output) is an effective mitigation.
paraphrase: At this capability level, automated monitoring of explicit reasoning output is believed to be an effective mitigation.

section_heading: Mitigation Approach and Critical Capability Levels
excerpt: Once a model is capable of effective instrumental reasoning in ways that cannot be monitored, additional mitigations may be warranted—the development of which is an area of active research.
paraphrase: Once instrumental reasoning becomes unmonitorable, additional mitigations, still under active research, may be needed.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
locator: Table 2 / Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 / Deceptive Alignment CCL
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1. Column: Deceptive Alignment CCL
excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1: the instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness (ability to work out and use relevant details of its deployment setting) and stealth (ability to circumvent basic oversight mechanisms) such that, absent additional mitigations, we cannot rule out the model significantly undermining human control.
paraphrase: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 is defined by sufficient situational awareness and stealth that, without mitigations, the model might significantly undermine human control.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1. Column: Mitigation
excerpt: Automated monitoring: a monitoring system to detect illicit use of instrumental reasoning capabilities in a model’s chain-of-thought and use it in high-stakes deployments where there is significant risk of the model undermining human control.
paraphrase: Mitigation is automated monitoring of chain-of-thought to detect illicit instrumental reasoning use in high-stakes deployments.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
locator: Table 2 / Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 / Deceptive Alignment CCL
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2. Column: Deceptive Alignment CCL
excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2: the instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness and stealth that, even when relevant model outputs (including, e.g., scratchpads) are being monitored, we cannot detect or rule out the risk of a model significantly undermining human control.
paraphrase: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 is defined by capability sufficient that even monitored outputs cannot detect or rule out significant undermining of human control.

section_heading: Table 2: Deceptive Alignment CCLs and Mitigations
context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2. Column: Mitigation
excerpt: Future work: We are actively researching approaches to addressing models that reach this CCL.
paraphrase: For this CCL, mitigation approaches are still under active research.

excerpt: Looking forward, we expect the approach to deceptive alignment risks to take a similar form as the deployment mitigation process.
paraphrase: The deceptive alignment approach is expected to resemble the deployment mitigation process.

excerpt: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
paraphrase: This introduces recommended actions for AI developers for each deceptive alignment risk.

context_stem: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
excerpt: Develop a safety case based on the model’s capabilities and the mitigations applied and tested.
paraphrase: Developers should build a safety case based on model capabilities and tested mitigations.

context_stem: Develop a safety case based on the model’s capabilities and the mitigations applied and tested.
excerpt: Such safety cases would make the case that the likelihood of deceptive alignment risk would be low enough for safe deployment, even if the model were trying to meaningfully undermine human control.
paraphrase: The safety case would argue the risk of deceptive alignment is low enough for safe deployment even under adversarial assumptions.

context_stem: For each deceptive alignment risk, AI developers should:
excerpt: Test the mitigations applied to models via red-teaming protocols called “control evaluations,” to determine whether they meet the requirements of the safety case.
paraphrase: Developers should test mitigations via control evaluations to see if they meet the safety case's requirements.

excerpt: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
paraphrase: The approach depends on two distinct safety case claims.

context_stem: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
excerpt: A model does not meet a threshold CCL and therefore would be incapable of substantially undermining human control.
paraphrase: Claim one: the model does not meet a threshold CCL and thus cannot substantially undermine human control.

context_stem: The approach above relies on two safety cases centering respectively on the claims that:
excerpt: An automated monitoring process that is validated by a control evaluation is adequate for catching the model’s malicious behavior.
paraphrase: Claim two: a control-evaluation-validated automated monitoring process is adequate to catch malicious behavior.

excerpt: Once neither of these apply, that is, once automated monitoring is no longer adequate/can no longer pass a control evaluation, a model is deemed to have reached the second CCL.
paraphrase: When neither safety case applies (monitoring no longer adequate or fails control evaluation), the model is deemed to have reached the second CCL.

excerpt: For Google models, when alert thresholds are reached, the response plan will be reviewed and approved by appropriate corporate governance bodies such as the Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council, Google DeepMind Responsibility and Safety Council, and/or Google Trust & Compliance Council.
paraphrase: Upon alert threshold triggers, the response plan is reviewed and approved by named corporate governance bodies.

excerpt: The Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council will periodically review the implementation of the Framework.
paraphrase: The AGI Safety Council will periodically review Framework implementation.

excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate the development of safe AI.
paraphrase: If a CCL poses unmitigated material risk to public safety, Google aims to share information with relevant government authorities.

excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
paraphrase: This introduces categories of information that may be disclosed, subject to confidentiality safeguards.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Model information: characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities.
paraphrase: One disclosable category is model information relevant to the risk posed by its critical capabilities.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
paraphrase: Another disclosable category is evaluation results, including design, results, and robustness tests.

context_stem: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
paraphrase: Another disclosable category is mitigation plans and their expected risk reduction.

excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organizations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
paraphrase: Disclosure to other external organizations may also be considered to promote shared learning and coordinated mitigation.

excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved.

excerpt: We expect the Framework to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves, and we will publish substantive revisions as appropriate.
paraphrase: The Framework is expected to evolve substantially, with substantive revisions published as appropriate.

excerpt: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
paraphrase: This introduces a list of issues planned for future Framework versions.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:

paraphrase: Future work includes improving estimation of attainable capabilities by threat actors, accounting for post-training enhancements.

context_stem: Issues that we aim to address in future versions of the Framework include:
